newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-ORGANISERS SCRAP EUROPEAN CUP FINAL DATE.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-ORGANISERS SCRAP EUROPEAN CUP FINAL DATE.

text.p: The uncertainty surrounding rugby union's European Cup increased on Thursday when it emerged that the final has been postponed to an undetermined date.

The expanded competition, featuring clubs and provinces from England, Scotland, Wales, Ireland, France and Italy, had been scheduled to reach a climax on January 4 with the semifinals being played in mid-November.

Now, to suit television who wanted more high-profile matches, a quarter-final round has been added with the semifinals switched to the first Saturday in January. A decision on where and when the final is played will be delayed until after the semifinals.

Organisers are still hunting for a host broadcaster in Britain after ITV's withdrawal this week. Rugby sources said ITV were still prepared to screen the matches to publicise the tournament but would not be paying for them.

Welsh Rugby Union chairman Vernon Pugh said negotiations were still continuing with other broadcasters and the chief sponsors, but reiterated the 20-team tournament, as well as the European Conference, would start as planned on October 12.

Pugh admitted there had been concern from France over recent developments and suggested some representatives of leading English clubs, who have been reluctant to commit themselves to the tournament, should stop rocking the boat.
"We have had a process of destabalisation that has been in place for more than 12 months," said Pugh.
"The French were concerned about any prospect of the tournament being devalued, but I was able to assure them they would be getting a feed of the matches in Britain.
"They see the European Cup as being very significant. I would have thought clubs like Leicester and Bath would want to prove they're the best in Europe."
Lions coach Ian McGeechan and French counterpart Jean-Claude Skrela are among those who think the tournament will be of immense value if the clubs treat it seriously.
"It's very important for clubs in the northern hemisphere to recreate the quality of rugby being played in the southern hemisphere," said Skrela.
"The European Cup offers a level of intensity between club and international rugby which should allow our players to make the step up more easily."
